articles.title: To Whom “Whom” May Concern: How Ellen Jovin Got People Across America Talking About Grammar
articles.content:
Suffering from punctuation paralysis? Semicolon confusion? End-of-sentence prepositions rage? Relax! The grammar guru, aka Ellen Jovin, will see you now. Or maybe she saw you already. Jovin has set up her Grammar Table in all 50 states, taking on every question posed by passersby, from the basic they’re vs. their to the eternally vexing lay vs. lie. And what she’s learned in her travels is this: Grammar is everywhere. We can’t escape it, even though many of us try. But love it, as Jovin does?
“I think it’s completely thrilling to be able to look at a sentence and know how many clauses and prepositional phrases there are, whether the verbs are transitive or intransitive, what the pronoun case is and so on,” she says. “I would have been ecstatic if we had spent additional years on grammar in school.”
In September 2018, Jovin, then an author, lecturer and communications coach for Syntaxis—her business that focuses on teaching communication workshops to businesses—was spending days cooped inside her apartment working on her language-learning blog as well as interacting in dozens of Facebook language groups. As the walls slowly began to close in on her, she had a revelation: I gotta get out of here!
“I didn’t want to spend that many hours a day online,” she says. Instead, “I wanted to use language in the real world for actual communication.”
So she stepped out of her apartment and set up a folding table across the street. Jovin, decked out in a leopard-print jacket, goofy ball-shaped earrings and a “Grammar Hedonist” T-shirt, was ready to laugh with everyone. She drew them little punctuation charts. She let them vent. As she told passersby: “I am here to answer grammar questions or take complaints.”

That December, she and her husband, Brandt Johnson, decided to take the show on the road, with Johnson filming what would become a documentary called Rebel with a Clause. True, he had never made a movie before. He’d done a lot of other things—acting, writing, even playing pro basketball in Europe touring against the Harlem Globetrotters. But mostly he and Jovin together run Syntaxis. That means they have the same boss—themselves—and could take off as soon as they wanted. So they did.
Those the couple met in their travels from Martha’s Vineyard to Flattop Mountain, Alaska, included kids, cops, lawyers, tourists, prom-goers, some grammar snob know-it-alls who got it all wrong, and two charming but inebriated young men with a pressing question. In Jovin’s book, also titled Rebel with a Clause, we meet Jason and Jack in Decatur, Alabama, after they’ve ambled over to her table to ask where the apostrophe goes in y’all. Jason wondered if it went before or after the a. Jack thought it didn’t go anywhere and y’all was just yall. Jovin explained that there is indeed an apostrophe and that it goes between the y and the all, because it’s taking the place of the rest of the word you.
The guys weren’t finished. While he and Jack helped themselves to her lunch, Jason asked what you call the “dot dot dot” you see when some words are missing.
“This is called an ellipsis,” said Jovin.
“I thought an ellipsis was the little …” Jason drew an oval in the air.
That’s an ellipse in math, Jovin explained. But in grammar it means something else and can be fun to talk about at parties. The plural is ellipses.
“I don’t normally talk to girls that are smart enough to know what that is,” Jason replied. “I need to find some girls that know what an ellipses is.”
He corrected himself: “What ellipses are.”
One sunny spring day in New York City, I accompanied Jovin to Central Park, where she set up her table and was soon swamped with queries.
“I still never get who and whom right,” said Linda Klein, a tourist from Los Angeles who was visiting with her dad, George Klein. “Do you have a trick for remembering it?”
Jovin smiled. She lives for such exchanges. While it all depends on context, she told Linda, there is a way to figure it out. Who is pretty much the equivalent of he, she and I—a subject. Whom is pretty much the equivalent of him, her or me—an object. And the way to figure which to use, Jovin continued, is to rephrase the sentence it’s in.
To use an example from Jovin’s book: If you’re trying to figure out what goes in the sentence “Evan, who/whom I thought was an honest person, plagiarized two paragraphs of mine,” you slice away everything outside of the commas. Then you consider whether you’d say “I thought he was an honest person” or “I thought him was an honest person.” Since it’s he, you use who.
But when it’s “Evan, who/whom I admired, just robbed a bank,” you take away what’s outside the commas and realize that Jovin admired him, not he. So you discover it’s whom, not who. Also that Evan is someone Jovin should steer clear of. (Yes—we’ll get to this point in a minute. It’s perfectly fine to end a sentence with a preposition, including of.)
Jovin and the Kleins continued to chat. Grammar is often an icebreaker, just as Jovin hoped. It turns out that George grew up in Czechoslovakia but also speaks Spanish (as does Jovin) and German (as does Jovin) and Hungarian, French and Russian (she’s got the French and a little Russian). Jovin has studied 28 languages and is currently brushing up on her Italian and Portuguese. She apologized to George for not having a Czech dictionary with her that day, though she did have a Polish one. Jovin always brings along a foreign language dictionary or two to help out in case people who speak those languages come to chat.
Linda had one last question: What does Jovin call herself? A therapist? “A roving grammarian,” Jovin answered.
As the Kleins were about to leave, another man strolled up. His name? Bill Funt. Was he possibly related to Alan Funt, creator of Candid Camera? Yup. That was his dad. This Funt was not fishing for the kind of squirmy moments that made his dad famous, but he did pose a couple of tough questions. First, he wondered if there was a nongendered word for aunt or uncle. After all, he said, the nongendered word for niece or nephew is nibling (a term coined by linguist Samuel E. Martin in the 1950s).
Jovin said she didn’t know of such a word, at least not in English.
“OK,” Funt continued. “My father, before he married my mom, was married and had three children. Then they divorced. Is there a word for what she [the first wife] is to me?”
“I have this same situation in my family,” Jovin replied. But there is, in fact, no special word, she said.
“In other words, I’ve stumped you twice!” said Bill, exultingly.
“But maybe the word you’re looking for doesn’t exist,” Jovin countered primly. “This is not a word-manufacturing plant.”
As Jovin and Johnson crisscrossed the country, certain grammar beefs and beliefs came up time and again. “I know people who will jump off a building before they split an infinitive,” Jovin says. An infinitive is the “to” form of a verb: To jump. To sigh. To barbecue. Those are infinitives. Fact is, there are times it is positively elegant to split them apart. Think of “to boldly go …”
As Jovin writes in her book, “The verb to go is the infinitive, and the adverb boldly intervenes.” It doesn’t sound bad—it sounds thrillingly Trekkian. But for eons, schoolkids have been taught to avoid it. Slaying that myth is something Jovin does almost daily.
She also deals with this one: A woman came up to her table to complain that the people who really need a grammar lesson probably never stop by. “My pet peeve is sentences ending in prepositions,” the woman said. “I see it all the time among people who should know better!”
The woman swanned off before Jovin had a chance to delicately explain that she should know better. Prepositions are little words that show relationships, like on the hill, at the hill, to the hill, up the hill. Never allowing them to end a sentence is another grammatical myth. This one somehow made its way into English via Latin, Jovin says. “But English is a Germanic language.”
Is it really better to say “That’s for what friends are” than “That’s what friends are for”? Or “Up to what are you?” instead of “What are you up to?” Ending a sentence with a preposition is not only grammatically kosher—it’s often required if you want people to understand what you’re driving at. Yes, at.
Another myth people cling to is that all adverbs—words that modify verbs—end in y. Words like slowly, snootily and bombastically do, of course. But the word often is also an adverb, as in “He’s often tripping over his toga.”
Jovin also has to deal with all the confusion over semicolons: Are they instead of a dash? A period? A comma? Yes. Basically, a semicolon is a way of connecting two ideas that could be separate but are also sort of linked; it’s also a way of making sure that phrases filled with commas have something bigger separating them.
So let’s move on to the battle royal of everyday grammar. The punctuation mark that starts brawls, ends dates and drives writers to drink. You know what I’m talking about: the Oxford comma, also known as the serial comma, also known as the series comma. It’s the much-debated practice of putting a comma before the and in a list.
Some publications, like the New York Times, swear by it. Other entities (we’re looking at you, Associated Press) recommend using series commas only when crucial for clarity. For instance, let’s look at this sentence: “I invited the ax murderers, Frank and Louie.” In that sentence, am I alone with the ax murderers, whose names are Frank and Louie? Or did I stupidly invite some ax murderers along with Frank and Louie? Putting a comma before and makes it me, Frank and Louie, scared for our lives. Without this clarifying comma, Frank and Louie are the ax murderers, and it’s just me with them. Yikes.
When a chemical engineering major stopped by the Grammar Table in Starkville, Mississippi, Jovin gave him a less-chilling example of this debate: “I ordered a salad, spaghetti and soda.” Would he put a comma after spaghetti? “Yes, definitely,” said the budding engineer. “It sounds weird otherwise, because if you say, ‘I ordered salad, comma, spaghetti and soda,’ it’s like spaghetti and soda are one entity. What is that? That’s nasty.”
Know what else is nasty? The lay vs. lie quandary. It’s just too confusing. Lie is something a noun or pronoun does: You lie down. The cow lies down. And lay is the past tense of lie. Fine. But! Lay is also the present tense of (and here’s where my head exploded) when you’re describing what someone did to a direct object: Gerry lay down his shrimp fork. Lenore lays her glasses on her head and then can’t figure out where she put them. Which, between you and I, just happened.
Wait, wait! That’s between you and me, not I! I vs. me is such a common mistake that it, too, must be mentioned here. “People think me is a dirty word,” Jovin says.
A student visiting the Grammar Table in Morgantown, West Virginia, told Jovin: “I know it’s right to say ‘Will you go to the bar with Emily and me?’ but I don’t want to sound stupid, so I say, ‘Will you go to the bar with Emily and I?’ ”
Jovin assured him that some people, including her, do know that me is absolutely right (and not stupid). The way to tell which word to use is, again, to strip away a lot of the sentence. Would you say “Go to the bar with I?” or “Go to the bar with me?” Me wins!
Maybe the biggest rule in the English language, says Jovin, is that nothing is set in stone, much to the chagrin of a certain demographic.
These days, Jovin hears older folks complain that their younger friends are saying “on accident” instead of “by accident.” The generations are also divided by the word like. You can, like, guess, which group uses it more and which group it, like, drives crazy.
And using they to denote a person who doesn’t want to be identified as he or she also requires some getting used to by the older generation. Especially since it’s singular, and hearing that “they” is coming over to do Jell-O shots begs the question of just how many Jell-O shots to prepare. (That said, they, even when denoting one person, still gets are, not the is treatment, Jovin notes.)
Like life, medicine and vacuum cleaners, grammar is always evolving. Usually, the older generation finds the younger one unutterably lax, while the young folk roll their eyes at their elders’ persnicketiness. “My feeling is that both generations should be tolerant of the other’s habits,” says the roving grammarian. “Every generation is innovative. They create their own words and terms, and it’s fun for them. It’s not a bad thing. It’s just what happens.”

articles.title: 77 Best Questions to Ask Relatives During Thanksgiving and Christmas to Learn More About Your Family History
articles.content:
The holidays are coming, which means family gatherings and at least one relative telling a story you’ve heard a hundred times. (You know the one.) But between the food and festivities, there’s an opportunity most of us overlook: learning more about our family history. After all, when else do you have so many people who know so much about your past gathered in one place? And we’re not just talking about digging up old family secrets (though those can be pretty juicy). Your relatives are living connections to people, places and stories you may never get another chance to hear about. The trick is knowing what family history questions to ask.
To help you get those conversations started, we tapped two experts from American Ancestors: David Allen Lambert, the company’s chief genealogist, and Sarah Quiat, the interim director for the Wyner Family Jewish Heritage Center. They shared the questions worth asking your relatives while you have the chance, whether you’re hoping to uncover surprising family stories or simply learn a little more about where you came from.
“Talking with relatives, especially those we see infrequently, allows them to reflect on their own lives and the lives of your shared ancestors before them,” Quiat says. “By passing what you learn from them to the next generation of your family, or to genealogical researchers, you create invaluable and unique sources of information that might not be found anywhere else.”
Read on for the questions to ask your relatives this holiday season, along with how to record them for future generations. You might be surprised by what you learn about your family—and yourself.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more holiday tips, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
The best way to start is to keep things casual. You don’t need to turn Thanksgiving dinner into a formal family interview to uncover great stories. Sometimes, a simple question like “How did you celebrate this holiday growing up?” is enough to get everyone talking. From there, you can ask about the relatives, traditions and memories that come up naturally.
If you want to preserve those stories, though, Quiat recommends hitting record. “Video recording is ideal, because you can see and hear someone telling their stories,” she says. And you don’t need fancy equipment. A smartphone works just fine, as long as your relative is comfortable being recorded.
For a more structured approach, set aside time for a one-on-one conversation, prepare a few questions and find somewhere quiet where you won’t be interrupted. Quiat also recommends getting permission on camera, as well as beginning with your names, the date, the location and what you’ll be discussing. You can bring out old photographs or family keepsakes to help spark memories too. And don’t feel you have to capture everything in one sitting. Consider your relative’s energy level, and remember that different family members may recall the same event differently, so it’s worth talking to several people.
Most importantly, don’t let the pressure to do it perfectly stop you from starting. As Quiat notes, “getting something is better than waiting to get it perfect and never getting the chance.”
The best way to uncover your family’s history is to ask the people who lived it, and the right questions can reveal surprising details you never knew about your relatives. According to Lambert and Quiat, here’s what to ask:
According to Quiat, one of the most important questions people forget to ask their relatives is: What advice would you give to future generations? “It can be of great value and insight to what was most important to the family member being interviewed, and it also actively brings the person listening into the picture,” she explains. It’s a chance to discover what your loved ones value most, what lessons they’ve learned and what wisdom they hope to pass down. Who knows? Their words might be exactly what a future grandchild needs to hear someday.
And don’t forget to dig into the little details behind your family’s biggest milestones. “Genealogists yearn for details, and an interview may reveal details about an event which you may only know names and dates,” says Lambert. For example, you might know when your grandparents got married, but do you know how they first met? Who made the first move? Lambert recommends asking relatives how they met their spouses or even how their own parents and grandparents fell in love. These conversations can uncover “a deep emotional memory that is never included in genealogical records and is often lost to time,” he says. After all, the dates might be written down somewhere, but it’s the stories behind them that really bring your family history to life.
Quiat and Lambert recommend capturing the kind of information you can’t easily find in records. articles.content:
Who would say no to a fancy royal title? I don’t know about you, but Your Royal Highness or even milady sound pretty great to me. Well, as it turns out, some titles are more of a curse than a blessing. In fact, there’s one title in the British royal family’s lineage that may literally be cursed!
We’re not just talking a little unlucky in love. We’re talking so bad that it’s effectively been banned from use. Yikes! Also, we’re totally intrigued, and we’re betting you are too.
So which title comes with a whole lot of baggage, and what happened to the royals to whom it was given? And could it ever be brought back from (ahem) the dead? We asked royal historian Tracy Borman, author of The Private Lives of the Tudors: Uncovering the Secrets of Britain’s Greatest Dynasty, to shed some light on the title no modern royal would likely ever want.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more royals, history, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
The Duke of Clarence. It’s a “rare title,” Borman explains, and notable because of the way its three doomed holders died. “Each of them met a fairly sudden and unfortunate death,” she explains. We’ll get to that in a minute, but first, a little history about how this title came to be.
This duchy was created by King Edward III in 1362 for his third son, Lionel of Antwerp. But while it seems safe to say that the monarch had good intentions, it brought Lionel everything but luck, and the “curse” started with him, its very first holder. Lionel was in his early 20s when he received the title. And given his age, he still had his life ahead of him—or at least that’s what he and his family thought. But nobody could have imagined what happened soon after.
They all died way before their time—and in very unusual circumstances. Coincidence or curse? Keep reading, and decide for yourself.
King Edward III’s third son was born in Antwerp (hence, the name) and married Violante Visconti, daughter of Galeazzo II Visconti, the Lord of Milan. Six years after becoming the Duke of Clarence—and only a couple of months into his second marriage, to Violante—he passed away.
“He was just shy of his 30th birthday,” Borman says. “And he died so suddenly that it was believed he’d been poisoned by his father-in-law.” Let’s just say the Visconti family had a reputation for ruthlessness and the whole “ends justify the means” mentality. Still, there’s no actual confirmation that Lionel’s death was the result of foul play.
Next came Thomas of Lancaster, second son of King Henry IV. He received the duchy when he was 24 or 25, in 1412. But this pairing was not meant to be. Borman notes that he was “very active on the battlefield and in government,” and he died while defending his country—but not particularly well. “He led the English in one of their most disastrous defeats to the French at the Battle of Baugé,” she says. “It was a fairly ill-advised attack, and he was killed at the age of 33.”
The most famous Duke of Clarence was George Plantagenet—brother of King Edward IV and King Richard III—who died a rather spectacular death at age 28. “He was the classic middle son of the three brothers, a kind of traitorous character who was not at all trusted by either of his siblings,” says Borman.
George tried to dethrone his brother Edward IV, who then had him convicted for treason. “Famously, it’s said that the Duke of Clarence was able to choose the manner of his death, so he decided to be drowned in Malmsey wine, which was, apparently, his favorite wine,” Borman says. While there’s no proof that this actually happened, “he’s definitely gone down in history for that.”
Technically, yes, but neither of them held the exact title Duke of Clarence—the two that got away both had extended versions of it. Plus, their lives weren’t all that rosy, as you’ll see.
Prince William Henry (1765–1837), also known as Duke of Clarence and St. Andrews, and later as King William IV, died of old age at 71. However, tragedy (and royal scandals) struck his home decades earlier: A notorious womanizer, William Henry had no less than 10 secret children with his mistress Dorothea Jordan, but he was pushed into marrying a more suitable woman, Princess Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen. The royal couple had two daughters together, but they both died in infancy.
The other one who escaped a mysterious death was Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence and Avondale (1864–1892). He died young, at the age of 28, but he was simply a victim of an influenza pandemic. That being said, rumor has it that he carried a dark secret. “Some authors have theorized that he was London’s serial killer Jack the Ripper,” Borman says. Wait, what?! The famous killer, of course, terrorized East London in the late 1800s. He murdered at least five women, all of them prostitutes, and was never caught. Jack the Ripper’s identity is still a mystery today.
No. “It died out, as sometimes happens with ill-fated titles,” says Borman. While there’s no official explanation for this—and monarchs have generally been free to choose whatever title they wanted for their kids—Borman thinks the reason is likely because “there were three fairly bad ends met by Dukes of Clarence, [and] it’s therefore a title people didn’t really want.”
This doesn’t mean that the royals are particularly superstitious, although she adds, “historically, they probably were a bit.” Let’s be honest: Even if you don’t believe in curses, would you really take the risk and give that title to a loved one? The number of untimely deaths aside, there could be another reason why monarchs have shied away from the title. “The last real Duke of Clarence, George, was so notorious and such an enemy to the Crown that the idea of creating another Duke of Clarence was pretty abhorrent,” Borman says. Fair point!
Yes, but considering what happened to the previous holders, it seems highly unlikely. Rumor had it for a while that Kate and William’s youngest son, Prince Louis, could be named the next Duke of Clarence once William becomes king. But this probably won’t happen. “Historically speaking, you’ve got to be careful with titles,” Borman says. “If there’s any negative association, then people can be quite cautious about bringing them back.”
Plus, we just can’t imagine that Kate or William would want their son associated with a late duke who got drowned in liters of wine and another who tried to overthrow the reigning monarch—and his own brother!

articles.title: Everyone’s Talking About You Can See Everything—Here’s Why the Twisty Elizabeth Holmes Documentary Is the Movie to Watch This Year
articles.content: If you could turn a camera on yourself in a movie theater, what would you see? If you’re watching the new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything, like I did last week, your face would probably be a mix of shock, bemusement, anger and overall slack-jawed incredulity at how we arrived at this moment in time. Like, what is even happening here? This strange movie about an equally strange character is mesmerizing, just like Holmes’s deep-welled, occasionally blinking blue eyes that have become a fixture over the last decade or so of her rise and fall. It’s a movie you can’t stop starting at, even as you want to avert your gaze, because it raises so many uncomfortable questions about our current moment, what we value and even reality itself. The A24 production, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, opened last weekend with a $15 million box-office haul, the biggest opener for a documentary since Michael Moore’s Fahrenheit 9/11 back in 2004. It did even better in its second weekend, bringing the doc’s two-week total up to $45 million. It’s also generating Oscar buzz and, due to its novel structure and storytelling technique, debate about whether it can even be considered a documentary at all. It’s a film that has everyone talking, and you do not want to miss it. Even though it’s nearly three hours long, I’d see it again right now if I wasn’t working. To get you ready to watch the film or discuss it with your friends, we scoured the web for helpful background info, hot takes and the buzziest debates about You Can See Everything. Read on to learn what all the fuss is about and what it says about our world right now. Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more entertainment, trends, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long. You Can See Everything follows Elizabeth Holmes, the co-founder of Theranos, a company that purported to invent a way to test a single drop of blood for a range of conditions, as she prepares to go to prison for defrauding investors. A darling of the tech industry back in the early 2010s, Holmes was hailed as the youngest female self-made billionaire and became the face of the rapidly emerging confluence of tech and medicine. The title of the documentary comes from a text message Holmes sent to Fielder, who also appears on camera throughout the film. She and her partner, Billy Evans, with whom she shares two young children, invite Fielder into their home in an attempt to rehabilitate her image, giving the filmmaker wide latitude to document their day-to-day lives. “You can totally see everything,” she texts to Fielder. But can we? As the movie unspools, that initial (some might say feigned) openness begins to feel like a pretext—or even duplicitous. If you’re familiar with Nathan Fielder, you might think he’s a curious choice for a celebrity rehab. And you’d be right. He’s best known as the creator and star of Comedy Central’s Nathan for You, a satirical take on those shows where business consultants help struggling companies succeed. His signature deadpan affect is on full display in You Can See Everything, his first full-length documentary, as is his ability to go well beyond the surface to expose something deeper. Still, Holmes’s artifice became confusing during the shoot, even for him. “I remember having this weird experience … where I’m like, she seems so genuine at times,” Fielder told the audience at a New York Film Festival panel discussion. “But then I’m like, no … I know she’s a liar. It was a weird mental thing.” Audiences for You Can See Everything will likely vary widely. It’s for people who remember the Theranos scandal, for those who are more interested in what Fielder is up to here and, of course, for anyone who wants to join in on the biggest conversation of the moment. It’s a quiet film, but there are plenty of times when I legitimately laughed out loud at its audacity. You Can See Everything is hard to describe, but if you like movies that make you think and have a point of view, get yourself to the theater ASAP. Opinions are overwhelmingly positive yet all over the map, with lots of words like bonkers and mind-bending being floated around. It’s everywhere too: Critics can’t get enough, and the internet is going crazy over the film’s inventive and ironic look at tech culture, our always-online viral reality and moviemaking itself. People are gravitating to it because it’s so much more than a documentary about a disgraced tech billionaire. Here are some highlights and links to great discussions about this fascinating movie. Be aware that there are some spoilers here, so jump ahead if needed. Here’s what everyone is saying about You Can See Everything. A24, the production company behind arthouse megahits like Moonlight, Backrooms and Primetime, has another disruptor on its hands here, and it’s perfect for audiences who are looking for something meatier than the latest superhero sequel. One through line running through A24 movies is the tendency to make small, indie films feel relevant to a broad audience, and this one delivers in spades. Variety‘s Owen Gleiberman says You Can See Everything is “everything a great movie should be: an experience unlike one you’ve had before, one that lures and enthralls you, and that leaves you feeling different when it’s over.” He compares the excitement to early rock ‘n’ roll and the 1970s film renaissance, when new and evolving art forms were transcendent. It’s “an ecstatic disruption, an adventure of the spirit, one that wakes you up and startles you, that makes you want to see it again.” Read more on Variety You read that right: You Can See Everything has already shot to the top of multiple Oscar-contender lists, and not in the Best Documentary category (though that’s a possibility too). Could it upend The Odyssey‘s chances? Maybe! A documentary has never even been nominated for Best Picture, which gives you an idea of how transformative this movie is. And it feels particularly relevant in today’s post-truth era, with Holmes insisting she did nothing wrong and Fielder’s astonishment channeling the audience’s disbelief. Of course, Oscar voters are not exactly known for embracing the avant-garde. But like 2020’s Parasite, the first foreign-language film to win Best Picture with its scathing critique of wealth inequality, and last year’s Sinners, a horror flick that nabbed four wins and 16 nominations, You Can See Everything could be another film that drags the Oscars into the modern era. Read more on The Los Angeles Times There is a shocking and rather sad moment in You Can See Everything that gets to the very heart of what Fielder is seeking to answer with this film: Is Holmes lying about her role in the Theranos scandal, or does she really believe that she did nothing wrong? Put another way, are we watching a performance? After pressing Holmes on her insistence that her blood-testing technology works as advertised, which clearly is not true (hence, her pending imprisonment), Fielder shows her Abbott and Costello’s “Who’s on First?” comedy bit, which plays with the idea of communication and misunderstanding. She doesn’t get the nearly century-old joke, just like she doesn’t seem to “get” that her tech really can’t do what she says it can. Or does she? How can two people who are living in the same reality see things so differently? In an era defined by second-guessing what’s real, from social media to politics to technology, “[Fielder’s] film is a self-reflexive study of the inability to act as people expect—of masking and deception,” says Coleman Spilde at Salon. “How much of life is a performance?” Read more on Salon In an era of streaming ubiquity, it’s been hard for studios to capture the attention of audiences who would just as soon stay at home—especially for a three-hour documentary. But in its opening weekend, You Can See Everything sold out more than 2,000 shows and raked in $15 million at just 855 theaters. After expanding to 2,600 theaters in its second weekend, it added another $19.5 million to its tally. Moviegoers are saying it’s one of those shared cultural moments you have to see in a crowd. Just take a quick look at your socials to see videos of packed lobbies and excited viewers who can’t wait to talk about what the heck they just saw. Read more on Mashable and The Guardian If you followed the Theranos scandal in real time, you likely have an unsympathetic opinion of Holmes. But here, both her partner, Evans, and Theranos co-founder Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, who was also convicted of fraud, come off as controlling and dominating. Late in the film, a reveal about Evans’s role in the negotiations, as well as his activities while she’s in prison, raise questions about who is the real villain here. But whistleblowers like Tyler Shultz, a Theranos employee who exposed her fraud, caution against buying into the victim narrative. The entire thing is messy, which is resonating with audiences who understand that life operates in the gray, not the black and white. Is it possible to have empathy for Holmes and, at the same time, see her as a manipulator? The movie seems to say yes. Read more on Yahoo! and NPR One of Fielder’s trademarks is his ability to hold a gaze for an excruciatingly long time. Pair that with Holmes and her tendency to do the same, combined with her wide-open eyes and constant nodding, and it’s immensely uncomfortable. Clips and memes of these stare-downs are all over the internet right now. Clinical psychologist and body-language expert Morgan Starr-Riestis has seen the film twice and says it’s unsettling. “When our eyelids are pulled back like that and we’re unblinking, that’s usually a sign of fear or overwhelm,” she told Today. “When you pair it with a smile, the mismatch is naturally unsettling. Our nervous systems just register it as something off.” A psychotherapist on Instagram, Elliot Connie, takes aim at Holmes’s selective nodding and head tilts, which he says are attempts to persuade and control the listener—usually Fielder, and by extension, the audience. Connie says these quirks are employed to make her seem docile and helpless but come off as deliberate and manipulative. Read more on Today and Instagram If you don’t want a spoiler about a major development in the second half of the film, skip to the next section! Everyone else, here we go: Fielder spends much of the movie documenting Holmes in the run-up to her reporting to prison. But things really get intense once she’s inside—and, of course, film crews aren’t allowed in Texas prison camps. So Fielder employs a ringer: Amanda Seyfried, who famously portrayed Holmes in The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu limited series based on the ABC News podcast of the same name. Seyfried doesn’t just read Holmes’s side of her conversations with Fielder—she also becomes part of the story, helping him piece together what’s going on with Evans on the outside. She’s so good at this strange double role that she’s being talked about as a potential Oscar nominee for Best Actress. Read more on The Daily Beast But wait—there’s more! We’ve rounded up additional links to explore if you want to go down the You Can See Everything rabbit hole. The entire thing is messy, which is resonating with audiences who understand that life operates in the gray, not the black and white. Is it possible to have empathy for Holmes and, at the same time, see her as a manipulator? The movie seems to say yes.

The stare-downs are completely transfixing

One of Fielder’s trademarks is his ability to hold a gaze for an excruciatingly long time. Pair that with Holmes and her tendency to do the same, combined with her wide-open eyes and constant nodding, and it’s immensely uncomfortable. Clips and memes of these stare-downs are all over the internet right now.

Clinical psychologist and body-language expert Morgan Starr-Riestis has seen the film twice and says it’s unsettling. “When our eyelids are pulled back like that and we’re unblinking, that’s usually a sign of fear or overwhelm,” she told Today. “When you pair it with a smile, the mismatch is naturally unsettling. Our nervous systems just register it as something off.”

A psychotherapist on Instagram, Elliot Connie, takes aim at Holmes’s selective nodding and head tilts, which he says are attempts to persuade and control the listener—usually Fielder, and by extension, the audience. Connie says these quirks are employed to make her seem docile and helpless but come off as deliberate and manipulative.

Fielder spends much of the movie documenting Holmes in the run-up to her reporting to prison. But things really get intense once she’s inside—and, of course, film crews aren’t allowed in Texas prison camps. So Fielder employs a ringer: Amanda Seyfried, who famously portrayed Holmes in The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu limited series based on the ABC News podcast of the same name.

Seyfried doesn’t just read Holmes’s side of her conversations with Fielder—she also becomes part of the story, helping him piece together what’s going on with Evans on the outside.
